\chapter{You're Welcome}
\label{ch:la-youre-welcome}
\hlchaptermodality{23}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can reply to thanks in Latin with nihil est, and say honestly how classical that reply is.}

Answer grātiās tibi agō with nihil est, and state plainly that the reply is modern convention built from real words.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[nihil est]{nihil est — \textquotedblleft{}you're welcome,\textquotedblright{} another honest gap}

\label{lesson:LA-C23-nihil-est}



\begin{quote}
You already learned that Latin has no fixed \textquotedblleft{}nice to meet you.\textquotedblright{} Here's the same honest gap again: no fixed reply to \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{} either.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: nihil est — \textquotedblleft{}it's nothing\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Nihil est} = literally \textquotedblleft{}{[}it{]} \textbf{is nothing}\textquotedblright{} — \textbf{nihil} (\textquotedblleft{}nothing\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{est} (\textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}). This is the phrase modern conversational-Latin communities commonly reach for as \textquotedblleft{}you're welcome,\textquotedblright{} parallel to English \textquotedblleft{}it's nothing\textquotedblright{} or Spanish \emph{de nada}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Nihil} itself is genuinely classical and richly attested, from an older \emph{\textbf{nihilum}}, itself built from \textbf{ne-} (\textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{hīlum} (\textquotedblleft{}a tiny thing, a trifle\textquotedblright{} — said to have originally meant \textquotedblleft{}the eye of a bean,\textquotedblright{} though its own ultimate origin is uncertain). So \textquotedblleft{}nothing\textquotedblright{} in Latin literally started life as \textquotedblleft{}not {[}even{]} a tiny bit\textquotedblright{} — the same shape of story as French's \emph{pas} (\textquotedblleft{}not,\textquotedblright{} originally \textquotedblleft{}a step\textquotedblright{}) or Spanish's \emph{nada} (from \emph{nāta}, \textquotedblleft{}a thing born\textquotedblright{}).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here's the careful part: \textbf{nihil} and \textbf{est} are both thoroughly classical, and \emph{nihil est} itself appears in real Latin texts — but always meaning things like \textquotedblleft{}there's nothing to it\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textquotedblleft{}nihil est, nūgae\textquotedblright{}}, \textquotedblleft{}nothing, trifles,\textquotedblright{} Plautus's \emph{Bacchidēs}) or \textquotedblleft{}that's nothing\textquotedblright{} (\emph{\textquotedblleft{}istuc quidem {[}edepol{]} nihil est\textquotedblright{}}, Plautus's \emph{Mīles Glōriōsus}), \textbf{never} specifically attested as a reply \textbf{to thanks}. No surviving Roman text shows someone answering \emph{grātiās agō} with \emph{nihil est}. Treat it the way you already treated \emph{quōmodo tē habēs?}: real Latin words, put to a genuinely useful modern job, but not a citation from a Roman play.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nihil est\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}it's nothing,\textquotedblright{} Latin's answer to \textquotedblleft{}thank you\textquotedblright{}
  \item nihil's own history — ne- + hīlum, \textquotedblleft{}not a tiny bit\textquotedblright{}
  \item the honest caveat — real words, modern job, not an ancient citation
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{nihil est} literally mean, and what job does it do here? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{{[}It{]} is nothing}\textquotedblright{} — the reply to \emph{grātiās agō}, \textquotedblleft{}thank you.\textquotedblright{}) What does \textbf{nihil} itself literally break down into? (\textbf{ne-} \textquotedblleft{}not\textquotedblright{} + \textbf{hīlum} \textquotedblleft{}a tiny thing\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}not a tiny bit.\textquotedblright{}) Is \emph{nihil est} specifically attested in a classical text as a reply to thanks? (\textbf{No} — a modern conversational-Latin convention built from real words, not an ancient citation.)
\end{tcolorbox}
